t: Beginning in 230 BCE, King Ying Zheng of Qin conquered Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and Qi in turn, and in 221 BCE took the new title Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor'.
The empire was divided into 36 commanderies and more than 1,000 districts run by appointed officials, ending aristocratic rule; the Han dynasty inherited this administrative state.
The dynasty's 14 years make it the shortest of any major Chinese dynasty, with only two emperors, yet it is credited with originating the imperial system that lasted until 1911.
dyk: Qin is the likeliest origin of the name China: the term appears in Sanskrit as Cina and Sina, then in Greek as Thinai or Sinai, before entering the languages of Europe.
ev: Qin attacks the state of Han directly to its east and takes its capital city of Xinzheng, opening the wars of unification.
Qin conquers Qi, taking its capital at Linzi, and King Zheng declares himself Shi Huangdi, the First Emperor.
The general Meng Tian conquers the Ordos region from the Xiongnu and agriculture is established there.
Some 500,000 men are sent south against the Baiyue peoples; after heavy losses, Qin takes the coastal lands around Guangzhou and the provinces of Fuzhou and Guilin.
Qin Shi Huang dies on a journey to the eastern frontiers; Li Si and Zhao Gao hide his death, alter his will and place Huhai on the throne as Qin Er Shi.
Popular revolt breaks out as men across China attack officials, raise armies and declare themselves kings.
Ziying, a son of Fusu, surrenders to Liu Bang on his arrival at Xianyang and is soon executed by Xiang Yu.
Xianyang is destroyed, marking the end of the imperial Qin dynasty; the Chu–Han Contention follows.

f.founder: Qin Shi Huang (Ying Zheng), the First Emperor
f.predecessor: The state of Qin, a fief of the Zhou dynasty, and the six rival Warring States it conquered
f.successor: The Eighteen Kingdoms, then the Han dynasty of Liu Bang (202 BCE)
